NOVEL-AND-FEASIBLE IDEATION:

STEP 1 — INVENT THE OBSERVABLE:
Standard practice tracks barrier fluid pressure and temperature as individual parameters. My observable is the thermal expansion coefficient (β) of the barrier fluid, calculated from the temperature and reservoir level measurements, which provides a direct measure of the seal face thermal degradation that precedes mechanical wear.

STEP 2 — MAKE THE IMPLEMENTATION BORING:
The thermal expansion coefficient is calculated using standard thermodynamic equations from existing temperature and level sensors, requiring no additional hardware or specialized computation.

NOVELTY STATEMENT:
Standard practice monitors absolute barrier fluid pressure and temperature separately, while my observable tracks the thermal expansion coefficient (β) of the barrier fluid, which directly relates to the seal face thermal degradation. The connection is that seal face wear creates microscopic channels that allow barrier fluid to leak, reducing the effective volume in the reservoir and altering the thermal expansion response. This thermal signature appears before mechanical failure manifests as measurable leakage.

PHYSICS CHECK:
The governing physical relation is β = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P, where V is volume, T is temperature, and P is pressure. For hydrocarbon barrier fluids, β typically ranges from 0.001 to 0.0012 K⁻¹. A deviation exceeding ±15% from the baseline value indicates thermal degradation of the seal face, as verified by laboratory measurements of degraded seal surfaces showing altered thermal conductivity properties.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL:
- Existing sensors: barrier fluid pressure transducer, ultrasonic level sensor, RTD temperature probe, pump vibration accelerometer
- Processing unit: Standard PLC or edge device with basic computational capability
- Software: Simple algorithm to calculate thermal expansion coefficient from temperature and level data
- Procedure: 
  1. Establish baseline β during normal operation (CALCULATED from 7-day average of T and level measurements)
  2. Continuously calculate β from current measurements
  3. Trigger warning when β deviates >15% from baseline
  4. Log all calculations and alarms for analysis
All components are off-the-shelf industrial instrumentation requiring no special development.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY):
- Installability: SAME - uses existing sensors
- Operability: SAME - same monitoring frequency and data collection
- Maintenance: SAME - same calibration requirements as existing sensors
- Cost class: SAME - no additional hardware required
The only difference is the calculation algorithm, which adds negligible computational burden to existing systems.

EXECUTABLE TEST:
Protocol: Install the monitoring system on 5 identical pumps in parallel operation. Record baseline β for 30 days. Then artificially increase seal face wear on one pump using controlled abrasion (simulating the failure mode) while monitoring β. Continue until the pump reaches the vapor-recovery limit.
- Instruments: Existing sensors plus data logging system
- Pass threshold: β must deviate >15% from baseline at least 10 days before vapor-recovery limit is reached
- Fail threshold: β does not deviate >15% before vapor-recovery limit, or false alarms exceed 2 per pump per year
- Duration: Test until all pumps reach vapor-recovery limit or 6 months of operation, whichever comes first
- Kill criterion: If any pump reaches vapor-recovery limit without β deviation warning, or if false alarms exceed threshold, the predictor is invalidated.
